standard.title: Comparing systems of government
standard.description: the key features and values of Australia's system of government compared with at least one other democratic or non-democratic system of government in the Asia-Pacific region
standard.prior_knowledge: Students know the role of the Australian Constitution in providing the basis for Australia's federal system and democratic processes, including institutions and the referendum process (AC9HC9K01). They understand the legislative processes through which federal government policy is shaped and implemented (AC9HC9K02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare the key features and values of Australia's system of government with at least one other system of government in the Asia-Pacific region, explaining similarities, differences and cultural influences.

nodes.label: Key features of Australia's system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the key institutional features and values of Australia's system of government, including free and fair elections, the party system, separation of powers, the rule of law, and protection of human rights.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain at least three key institutional features of Australia's system of government using accurate civics terminology.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full set of key features — elections, party system, partial separation of powers, rule of law, and human rights protections — and the democratic values underpinning them.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians have historically engaged with and been affected by Australia's political institutions, and compare with Indigenous peoples' political participation in another nation
Investigate how Australia's federal structure distributes power between Commonwealth and states, and trace how this emerged from colonial history
Explore the role of the Westminster tradition in shaping Australian democratic norms and compare with a presidential system
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot accurately characterise Australia's own system will make false comparisons in subsequent nodes — misidentifying similarities and differences based on misconceptions about the Australian baseline.

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate features (e.g. treating separation of powers as complete rather than partial) or conflate values with structures. Invest time unpacking the distinction between institutional mechanisms and underlying democratic values before comparison begins.
Width across multiple features (elections, law, rights protections) ensures students have a usable comparative framework rather than a single point of comparison.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of institutional features provides rich comparative entry points. Students who engage with First Nations political participation or the Westminster tradition's cultural roots build a more nuanced comparative framework for the following nodes.
success_criteria: Identifies and accurately describes at least three key features of Australia's system of government
Explains a democratic value that underpins at least one of those features
Uses appropriate civics terminology (e.g. separation of powers, rule of law)

nodes.label: Features of a comparison system
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the key features of at least one other system of government in the Asia-Pacific region, identifying whether it is democratic or non-democratic.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least three key institutional features of one selected comparison system, identifying whether it is democratic or non-democratic.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the key features of a selected Asia-Pacific system of government — including electoral processes (or lack thereof), structure of power, rule of law, and rights protections — and classify it as democratic or non-democratic with reasons.
wider: Investigate the political system of an additional Asia-Pacific nation to enable a three-way comparison
Examine how cultural, historical or colonial factors shaped the comparison system's current political structures
Research the experiences of Indigenous peoples in the comparison nation's political system and evaluate the degree of their inclusion

response_modes.reason: Students benefit from building a repertoire of examples from the Asia-Pacific region — even minimal exposure to two or three systems before selecting one for deep comparison gives them more informed selection criteria.

success_criteria: Describes at least three key institutional features of the selected comparison system
Classifies the system as democratic or non-democratic and provides at least one reason
Uses appropriate civics terminology to describe the comparison system

nodes.label: Structured comparison
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the key features and values of Australia's system with the selected comparison system, identifying specific similarities and differences across multiple dimensions.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two similarities and two differences between Australia's system and the comparison system, using a structured framework (e.g. table, structured paragraph).
nodes.typical_width: Compare Australia's system with the selected system across multiple dimensions — electoral processes, structure of power, rule of law, and rights protections — explaining both structural differences and the values that underpin them.
wider: Compare the experiences of First Nations Australians in engaging with the Australian political system with those of Indigenous peoples in the comparison nation
Evaluate which system better protects human rights for minority groups, drawing on specific evidence
Investigate how global interconnectedness (international agreements, trade, migration) has influenced political similarities between the two systems
nodes.hinge_reason: The comparison move is the core demand of this descriptor. Students who produce surface-level comparison (listing features without connecting them to underlying values) will not satisfy the descriptor's 'key features and values' framing — the integration node cannot recover this gap.

response_modes.reason: Students often list differences without explaining the values or institutional logic behind them. Use structured scaffolds (e.g. comparative frameworks) to push students from feature-matching to values-based analysis.
Widening to include First Nations political participation or rights-minority analysis gives students comparison across multiple values dimensions, not just structural features.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations political participation and human rights comparison are pedagogically rich directions that deepen students' understanding of democratic values rather than just institutional structures. These are substantive rather than decorative enrichment directions.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two structural similarities and two structural differences between the two systems
Connects at least one difference to an underlying democratic or non-democratic value
Uses specific evidence or examples from both systems to support the comparison

nodes.label: Cultural influences on political systems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural influences have shaped Australia's political system and that of the comparison country, reflecting on what this reveals about the relationship between culture and governance.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one cultural or historical influence that has shaped Australia's political system and one that has shaped the comparison system.
nodes.typical_width: Explore and reflect on the cultural, historical and social influences shaping both political systems, explaining how these influences account for key differences in values and institutional design.
wider: Investigate how colonialism has shaped political institutions in both countries and the ongoing implications for First Nations or Indigenous peoples
Compare how religious, philosophical or ethnic diversity is managed differently in each system and what this reveals about democratic values
Examine how recent political change (e.g. constitutional reform, protest movements) reflects cultural values in one of the two nations

response_modes.reason: This node integrates feature knowledge, comparative skills, and cultural reasoning into a reflective account. Students are synthesising earlier nodes rather than adding new factual content — the teaching investment is in supporting that synthesis.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific cultural or historical influence on each system's political design
Explains how that influence connects to a visible feature or value of the system
Reflects on what the comparison reveals about the relationship between culture and governance
